title: CHAPTER FIVE. On Sacred Scripture's perfection and sufficiency
english:
CHAPTER FIVE
On Sacred Scripture's perfection and sufficiency

So far concerning Sacred Scripture's authority: next comes perfection, which is its property by which the catholic principles of sacred doctrine common and necessary to all Christians, set out wholly and purely partly in the Hebrew tongue and partly in the Greek, are so sufficiently embraced that nothing ought to be added and nothing subtracted ([[Deuteronomy 4:2 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 4:2]]; [[Proverbs 30:6 >> Bible:Proverbs 30:6]]; [[2 Corinthians 2:17 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 2:17]]; [[Revelation 22:18 >> Bible:Revelation 22:18]]-[[Revelation 22:19 >> Bible:Revelation 22:19]]).

So also Aristotle, On the Heavens book 2 chapter 4, defines the perfect as that to which nothing is lacking and outside which nothing of the things that belong to it can be taken. And this the nature of a canon requires, which Varinus defines as μέτρον καὶ κριτήριον — an infallible measure admitting no addition or diminution.
This perfection of the sacred canon is certain (1) as to the number of canonical books, (2) as to the purity of the authentic text, (3) as to the integrity of the lettering.

title: As to the number of canonical books: none needful to salvation has perished; against Bellarmine and Becanus
english: First, as to the number of canonical books: none needful to us for salvation have perished. For Bellarmine is false when he says (On the Word of God book 4 chapter 4): "Many truly sacred and canonical books have perished. Therefore we do not have, nor have we had for 1500 years, sufficient doctrine, if the whole of it is seated in the Scriptures."

The antecedent is false, as is plain from considering the eighteen books Becanus brings forward as lost from the canon. For by God's singular providence the canonical books have been so kept that not even a jot, much less a whole book, could perish from the canon ([[Matthew 5:18 >> Bible:Matthew 5:18]]).

Of the books Becanus and other papists complain are lost, we note: (1) some still remain in the canon today; (2) some never existed; (3) some were not books but recensions; (4) some are historical works whose prophetic spirit is not established; (5) some are forensic books, as interpreters will have it.

title: As to authentic-text purity: the Hebrew was not corrupted in the prophets', Apostles', or Jerome's ages
english: Second, Sacred Scripture is perfect as to the purity of the authentic text. Ours have shown this clearly, and against Gordon Huntly's blasphemies the most learned Salomon Glassius especially has solidly proved it in his Sacred Philology.

For the Hebrew text of the Old Testament was not corrupted in the prophets' time: they knew they were not allowed to change or innovate even the least thing in the law (as the Talmudists note at the end of Leviticus 27); nor would they have suffered that crime to be done by others; nor could corruption have been attempted in the authentic exemplar without them.

Nor was it corrupted from the prophets' time onward: because already from Ezra the Masora was added, and because Christ and the Apostles, most sharp-eyed Aristarchuses of false interpretations of the law, would without doubt have noted a corruption of the context if there had been any — as Origen on Isaiah book 8, Jerome on Isaiah 6, and Augustine City of God 15.13 urge. Nor from the Apostles' time: whether we look to the megilloth-sopher ([[Psalm 40:8 >> Bible:Psalm 40:8]]) and the Hebrews' handwritten Bibles, or to the Masora, we find nothing but God's marvelous providence and the Jews' stupendous fidelity and most exquisite diligence in guarding the Bibles — of which Josephus Against Apion and Eusebius Church History 3.10 testify that any Jew would rather die a hundred times than suffer the law to be changed in any point.

Nor in Jerome's age (Ribera on Hosea 9: if the codices were then corrupted when Jerome published the Latin translation, the church does not have the true Scripture). Nor in today's Jewish manuscript Bibles — so great is the consent that not even one book of Scripture written by a Jew's hand can be produced that either lacks something the others have or adds what the others lack.

title: Sixtus of Siena: divine Old Testament Scriptures not falsified; five observations against corruption charges
english: From all this, judgment is made about the printed exemplars we still use, whose typographical slips are known to the learned. Hence Sixtus of Siena (Bibliotheca book 8, heresy 2) says it cannot be said that the divine Scriptures of the Old Testament have been falsified by the malice of Jews or of Christians.

For greater clarity of the matter, let these be observed: (1) Not every change proves corruption. Hence Benedictus Arias Montanus in the preface to volume 1 of the Bibles says the Hebrew books we use were not corrupted by Jewish fraud; and even if some change was made, yet no word or letter or point ever existed that was not observed in the Masoretic tradition. (2) The papists deal with such Old Testament corruption in order that the Latin Vulgate version may flow purer than its source. They will demonstrate that on the Greek Kalends. (3) Corruption asserted by some fathers rests not on demonstration but on suspicion. For they were ignorant of the Hebrew tongue — unless perhaps you except Justin lightly tinged with these letters, and Origen and Jerome excellently steeped in them, who with us vindicate the Hebrew text from corruptions. (4) Many fathers complain of corruption not of the sources but of the versions of the Seventy, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and others. (5) The suspicion of corruption rests on the papists' false hypothesis pronouncing the Latin version authentic, so that no one dares reject it under any pretext (Council of Trent session 4).

title: As to integrity of the lettering: the claim that vowel points were added late after Christ
english: Third, Sacred Scripture is perfect as to the integrity of the lettering. Some among the Jews, and those among Christians who follow them in this, think the Hebrew text only some centuries after Christ's birth attained the perfection in which it now shines, by the addition of vowel and distinguishing points — so Bellarmine On the Word of God book 2 chapter 2, Petrus Martinius, the Arcanum of punctuation revealed by Thomas Erpenius, Gordon Huntly, and most others today taught by Jewish instructors, who trust the histories of Elias Levita and certain other Jews.

But this assertion seems wholly to contradict the perfection of the holy tongue, which cannot be worse than all other languages, as if it were thought written by divine men with consonants alone without vowels — vowels that in every language animate and perfect every consonant.

title: Against late punctuation: the claim is unhistorical, suspicious in time, object, authors, and witnesses
english: Besides: (1) The claim is destitute of historical credit. For if the Masoretic correction and perfection of the points had been made after Jerome's time, as they will have it, some mention of so great a deed would doubtless have been inserted somewhere by the holy fathers — especially by Jerome's disciple-bishops who lived in the East skilled in Hebrew. How great the contests were over the version of the Seventy, Symmachus, Aquila, Theodotion, Jerome, Luther, Piscator, and Castalio is all too well known.

(2) It is suspicious as to time, object, authors, and witnesses. The time is after the New Testament canon was complete, when that Masoretic work is said to have been done — after which, since beforehand neither the Apostles nor their apostolic followers nor those who delivered it to the Church doubted even slightly about itly say that anyone either could or would have attempted so great a crime. The object — namely the biblical codex — was so sacred to the Jews that writing upon it was like a sacrilege. The authors would be rabbis, either bad or good. If bad, perhaps the canon's integrity will waver. If good, they would rather have died than add even a jot to the text. The witnesses are rabbis, whose faith is rather shaky, and they do not agree among themselves, as Münster testifies.

title: Late punctuation is dangerous: no need, no mandate, and no infallible sense if the points are new
english: (3) It is dangerous. First, because that change of the Bibles would have been made without necessity of the time, if it was made at all: both because God by His providence could have preserved the sacred Scripture He had kept until then into late ages without such an addendum, and because neither God's command nor any reason of necessity drove them to this work. For the author of the Arcanum of punctuation revealed (book 1 chapter 18) shows by many reasons that unpointed Hebrew could somehow be read of old, and today we know from Jewish manuscripts that they read the sacred texts most readily without points.

Second, because for so many ages back that would have stood in the authentic text of the Bibles which is not true in every part and does not belong to authenticity's majesty. For when the anonymous author (book 2 chapter 22) teaches that our judgment cannot finally and infallibly be fixed on those points, and that nothing ought to be concluded infallibly and authentically from the truth of sense that arises today from that placement and form of the points — then what has until now been held as belonging to the authentic text's literary integrity collapses and vanishes into air like an Empusa.

Third, because it will then be doubtful what the Holy Spirit properly intended in each place of Scripture, and we will not be able to know it infallibly. For we may not flee to the points we use today as to authenticity's asylum, because they are new, and the infallibility of the sense emerging from them is denied. Nor would one believe the punctators were prophets, since the rabbis are known to have been the fiercest enemies of the Christian name. Nor is it enough meanwhile to appeal to the letters: since these are formless, from where will they draw an infallible form? One will have to flee to a living or mute master: the former is not given, and if given would be fallible; the latter is wanting to this day. The Chaldee paraphrase is a version, not authenticity; the rabbis' darkness is a gulf of trifles; after Christ's ascension there is no synagogue — on that path the genuine sense would hang solely on the Jewish church, and Scripture would be a dead letter.

title: Late punctuation is contradictory on cause, place, and time; and contrary to Scripture's witness to points in Christ's day
english: (4) It is contradictory. First, as to the efficient cause — namely the Masoretes. For Buxtorf in his Tiberias and others think the points were added to the Bibles by men of the Great Synagogue — Ezra, Daniel, Zechariah, Malachi, Hananiah, Nehemiah, Zerubbabel, Joshua son of Jozadak, and so on — a council they call the Great Synagogue, in which they chiefly arranged the sacred books by the prophetic spirit they possessed and added the points to them. Others differ much from these and suspect the points were added to the bare bodies of the letters by exiled Jews after Christ's birth (Aaron of Asher's tribe and Jacob of Naphtali's at Tiberias). Finally some assign no certain authors, or are ignorant of them (Elias Levita in Buxtorf).

Second, as to place: this discrepancy depends on the former. Third, as to time: some refer the art of punctuation to what was immediately after the exit from Babylon before Christ was born; others after His birth, who yet themselves disagree (the years 236 / 436 after the temple's destruction, and so on).
(5) It is contrary to the Scriptures, because that the points existed in Christ's time is gathered from [[Matthew 5:18 >> Bible:Matthew 5:18]] and [[Luke 16:17 >> Bible:Luke 16:17]].

title: Scripture's witness to points continued: iota and tittle; late punctuation is impossible
english: The Scriptural argument continues from [[Luke 16:17 >> Bible:Luke 16:17]], where the keraia — the "tittle" or little horn — is distinguished from the jota, which is the least of the letters and therefore does not belong to their bare shape, as Erpenius holds in the Arcanum of revealed punctuation and Capellus in the Myrothecium. Rather it is beyond doubt the tiniest mark: among the vowels the upper holem, the middle segol, the lower hireq; among the accents, rebia. Nor may one take refuge here in the apices of the Samaritan Bibles and Scripture, of which Jerome speaks in the preface to the books of Kings. For besides the fact that that writing too is done without points, as some note, Christ speaks of the Law, and indeed of authentic Scripture which the Jews had received. Erpenius and Capellus deny that the tittle signifies some little body separate from the letters, and the rabbis do have certain keraiai — tagin, or little crowns — set on letters even in unpointed books; yet it is not likely Christ is so taken here, because a letter's flourish in writing often either perishes or is lengthened, and varies strangely at times. Christ's saying stands best if He is believed to have said: No letter, nor point, and so not even the least of them, will be changed in the Law.

(6) It is impossible. For those who assert the novelty of the points are driven either to say that certain points are missing from the letters, or to set up something analogous to them. Johannes Drusius (Animadversiones 2.60) does not deny that diacritical points occur in a codex before Jerome's time — after which the rabbis themselves say they undertook the work of pointing. Schickard, when in Mishpat ha-melekh he treats the writing of the royal Bibles in the Old Testament and explains a rabbinic saying that mentions pointed letters, says: The points it mentions here are not vowels and accents, but certain extraordinary points. For the rest, as those copies lack vowels, so in turn they have something else our codices do not know — namely very frequent apices, not arbitrary but in a fixed number and in due places, which they call tagin or little crowns, because as a beth stands high on kings' heads, so these stand out above the words.

title: Late punctuation is absurd: doubtful sense; confessors, reason, and examples; authentic versus private Bibles
english: (7) It is absurd. For if the novelty of the points stands, the sense of Scripture is most doubtful — which fights against the truth, simplicity, and immutability of the speaking God, and foists on one simple saying of sacred Scripture several literal senses, and therefore doubtful ones. This is proved in three ways.

First, by the confession of those who defend the novelty of the points. The author of the Arcanum of revealed punctuation (book 2, chapter 22) says: If some places of Scripture are brought forward in which varying pointing begets a varying sense, yet each true, fitting, apt, not badly cohereing with what goes before and after, and not against the analogy of faith — what danger will there be if here one embraces this pointing and with it this sense, another another pointing and another sense with it? Or what danger even if both senses that rise from it? None, he says. And Rabbi Bechai on [[Numbers 11:15 >> Bible:Numbers 11:15]]: Consonants, he says, without vowel points have various and ornate understandings; for which cause we have a precept not to add vowels to the book of the Law, because they would then have only one sense — whereas without them they admit various and wonderful significations.

Second, by reason. For as from the determination of subject and predicate by the copula one statement is made, so from the pointing of the words of the Hebrew text there is a determination to one sense, which, that pointing omitted, is often doubtful. Hence Münster: He who does not heed what is written above and below in the books perverts the words of the living God. And from Recanati: It is certain that when a letter is not pointed it can be read in various ways; but when points are added it bears only one sense, according to the form of the pointing. Therefore either the points together with the twenty-two letters are from the Author at once, or else Scripture was once flexible like soft wax, now this way, now that. And if the points were invented by men, it necessarily follows that Scripture in this our time has authority that is not divine — which is most absurd.

Third, by examples, which see in Engelbert's preface to Schindler's Pentaglot Lexicon. For the rest, one must distinguish between authentic and public Bibles and private ones. That the former were of old unpointed has not yet been firmly enough proved; that the latter were not all pointed we grant. For as difficulty made these lack points, so necessity of religion made those not lack them — witness Franciscus Junius in his Animadversions on Bellarmine.

title: Scripture's perfection as to what it contains: divine revelation and catholic dogmas of the faith
english: II. But it also embraces what is necessary — both insofar as divine revelation is the principal cause of knowing, and insofar as the catholic dogmas of the faith, or revealed propositions, on which religion properly rests, and which have the force of an infallible principle for framing further conclusions, are signified.

It is worth noting here that all who agree in these principles understood in either way are also to be judged to agree in the foundation of religion, and cannot properly be held heretics or unbelievers as far as doctrine is concerned — by the argument of [[1 Corinthians 3:15 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 3:15]]. But those who are ignorant of these principles, or deliberately dissent in them, are no more Christians than those who ignore or deny principles known by nature have commonly been sound.

III. Divine revelation we explained in Chapter 2. But a catholic dogma of the faith is elsewhere taken for a principle, elsewhere for any conclusion truly drawn from a principle — either manifestly and evidently, or not equally manifestly. In the former mode a dogma of the faith cannot be denied by any Christian; yet that can happen in the latter mode.

IV. Catholic dogmas, or the principles and foundations of the Christian religion, are called necessary either with respect to eternal salvation, or with respect to institution, or finally with respect to certainty.

title: Necessary dogmas: for eternal salvation, for church teaching, and for certainty
english: V. With respect to eternal salvation they are those that are simply necessary for obtaining salvation, and therefore must be ignored by none, but expressly held by all adults. Such are [[Hebrews 11:6 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:6]]: Whoever comes to God must believe that He is God and that He rewards those who seek Him. Which place Socinus himself in his Prelections refers to those to whom God has somehow made Himself known. For those, he says, unless they believe that God is, show that they have a mind alien from piety and so from the study of just and unjust.

VI. With respect to institution they are those that are necessarily expounded by all who teach in the Church, and therefore must be withheld by none, but handed on by all in the Church. Such are all and each of the heads of the Apostles' Creed. For it is probable that all that is contained in the Apostles' Creed is precisely necessary to salvation for all who are to be saved in the New Testament — at least as to the sense clearly expressed in other places of Scripture — even if they do not hold the Creed's wording and manner of interpreting. Hence these dogmas are also properly called articles of the faith. Yet because the consideration is different, and we cannot determine with sufficiently evident certainty which or how many heads of doctrine are precisely such that without express knowledge of them God wills to save no one, but more rightly commit this whole matter to the secrets of divine judgment — therefore this latter cause of the naming must somehow be distinguished from the former.

VII. With respect to certainty they are all those that have divine and universal evidence, and therefore, though ignored by many, yet once known must be denied or opposed by none, but necessarily granted. Such is every Word of God — not indeed absolutely, but what is catholically revealed, that is, so that the certainty of divine revelation can be understood by all if it is proposed, and once understood can never be denied without evident malice or unbelief and denial of God. And these are of such a kind as, beyond those that are absolutely necessary, and before the revelation of them is made, are said to be believed by the faithful with a certain preparation of mind. For Calvin aptly says (Institutes 3.2.4): But we grant that faith, as long as we pilgrimage in the world, is implicit — not only because many things still lie hidden from us, but because, surrounded by many fogs of error, we do not attain everything. For of the most perfect, whatever his height of wisdom, the sum is to advance, and with quiet teachableness to press farther.

title: All needful dogmas are perfectly contained in Old and New Testament Scripture; reasons from canon, testament, praises, and Isaiah
english: VIII. We therefore assert that all dogmas whose knowledge is necessary for salvation, for catechetical institution, and finally for certainty are perfectly contained in the books of the Old and New Testament, and sufficiently handed down — either expressly, as to the wording itself, or equivalently, as to likeness, by evident equipollence or by a legitimate and catholic consequence.

The reason for the perfection of sacred Scripture that we assert is, first, from the notion of a canon, because it sets forth a rule of the things that are for us to be believed and done ([[Galatians 6:16 >> Bible:Galatians 6:16]]; [[Philippians 3:16 >> Bible:Philippians 3:16]]). But a rule is a certain measure to which nothing can be taken away, nothing added, by private authority — which Gerson (tome 1, part 2, in the treatise On the examination of doctrine) wisely applied to the canon of sacred Scripture. And of this rule some parts are essential, some integral, and must be prudently distinguished. In the former the substance of things to be believed and done is looked to; in the latter the mode and manner of application. In the former rather than in the latter the force and nature of a rule is placed. And so the whole of Scripture indeed, yet not the whole of what is in Scripture, is established by us as a rule — just as in a material rule not everything that belongs to the rule is itself the rule.

Second, the same is proved by the notion of a testament, by which appellation those sacred books are designated ([[2 Corinthians 3:6 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]], 14; [[Galatians 3:17 >> Bible:Galatians 3:17]]; 4:24; [[Ephesians 2:12 >> Bible:Ephesians 2:12]]; [[Hebrews 9:15 >> Bible:Hebrews 9:15]]–17).

Third, from those praises which it has from its Author and from its efficacy ([[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]; [[Psalm 19:7 >> Bible:Psalm 19:7]]–8; [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]–16).

Fourth, from Isaiah's most weighty warning, calling everyone from human and diabolical inventions back to Mosaic and prophetic Scripture alone ([[Isaiah 8:20 >> Bible:Isaiah 8:20]]): To the law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, they have no dawn of light.

title: Further reasons for Scripture's perfection: Christ's judgment, spoken and written Word, Abraham, and the Apostles
english: Fifth, from the judgment of Christ, who for this cause exhorts the Jews to search the Scriptures — or at least approves that they set their study in searching them ([[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]]) — because in them He presents Himself wholly to be known, and brands ignorance of them as the mother of all errors ([[Mark 12:24 >> Bible:Mark 12:24]]), and sets them far above every other revelation, however miraculous ([[Luke 16:29 >> Bible:Luke 16:29]]).

Sixth, from the equating of the word pronounced and the word written, as equivalent helps which Christ and the Apostles used ([[Luke 24:27 >> Bible:Luke 24:27]]; [[Acts 17:2 >> Bible:Acts 17:2]]; 26:22; [[Philippians 3:1 >> Bible:Philippians 3:1]]; [[2 Thessalonians 2:15 >> Bible:2 Thessalonians 2:15]]; [[1 John 1:3 >> Bible:1 John 1:3]]–4; [[Luke 1:3 >> Bible:Luke 1:3]]–4; [[Acts 1:1 >> Bible:Acts 1:1]]).
Seventh, from Abraham's reply ([[Luke 16:29 >> Bible:Luke 16:29]]): They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.

Eighth, from the testimony of the Apostles, and from their precept by which they forbid us to be wise above what is written, and from their example by which from the Scriptures alone they confirm their doctrine, refute adversaries, and preach nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets had foretold ([[1 Corinthians 4:6 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 4:6]]; [[Acts 26:22 >> Bible:Acts 26:22]]).

Ninth, from the less probable. For if the Apostles themselves clung so tightly to the Scripture of the Old Testament, much more we, after that old canon has been enlarged by so lucid an interpretation and addition of the New Testament — we who are endowed neither with an equal measure of the Spirit nor with equal authority. And now the Scripture of the Old Testament is called a perfect law, imparting life ([[Psalm 19:7 >> Bible:Psalm 19:7]]; 119), wisdom and prudence ([[Deuteronomy 4:6 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 4:6]]; 17:19; 31:11–13).

title: Final reasons for perfection: Scripture's end, God's counsel, the canon's close, and orthodox antiquity
english: Tenth, from the end of the New Testament, and from the use of all Scripture for the man of God ([[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[Luke 16:29 >> Bible:Luke 16:29]]).
Eleventh, from the sufficient exposition of God's counsel concerning our salvation ([[Acts 20:27 >> Bible:Acts 20:27]]; 26:22; [[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]).

Twelfth, from the closing clause of the whole Christian canon ([[Revelation 22:18 >> Bible:Revelation 22:18]]–19), which John Scotus — not the least of the schoolmen, whom Scaliger calls the file of truth — rightly understood not of the Apocalypse alone but of all Scripture.

Thirteenth, from the consent of orthodox antiquity, from which Irenaeus truly and reverently says: The Gospel which they first preached they afterward, by God's will, handed down to us in the Scriptures, to be the pillar and foundation of our faith. And Tertullian: When we believe, he says, this we first believe — that there is nothing beyond which we ought to believe. I omit others. Those who do not hold and defend this strictly and tooth-and-nail, but decide and so propound their dogmas by the authority of whatever church, and finally resolve them into it — they fall from the first line of the Reformation and stand as near as can be to the old leaven of the papists, which they wish to appear to oppose and spit out.

title: First contradiction: papists equate unwritten tradition with Scripture; kinds of tradition
english: IX. To the perfection of sacred Scripture that we have explained, the papists first contradict, who equate tradition — or the unwritten word — with the written, and decree that the whole mass of their traditions must be received and believed with equal affection of piety together with the undoubted Word of God. See the Council of Trent, session 4, chapter 1; Bellarmine, On Justification 3.3. When James, bishop of Cloches, had called that decree hard, he was ordered by the pontiff to go to Rome to obtain pardon, as Paolo Vergerio reports in a letter to the king of Poland. By unwritten traditions, says Adam Tanner in the Ratisbon Colloquy, we understand certain precepts or constitutions pertaining to faith or religion which, the infallible authority of the Church set aside, are neither openly expressed in Scripture nor evidently deduced from it.

Note here the cover they stretch: (1) faith-dogmas; (2) moral institution; (3) observation of rites. Hence of traditions we can call some dogmatic, some ethical, and others hieratic or ritual. Dogmatic and ethical ones outside Scripture we receive none. For though not every particular of the Apostles was written — because we have neither knowledge nor number of the particulars — yet their common foundation, reason, and proof is contained in the Scriptures, in which the Church of Christ finds and recognizes the genera of particulars, even if not every particular of the genera. For singular narratives of the sayings and deeds of Christ and the Apostles that are read among the ancients, and that can be called historical traditions, must be judged from Scripture and held as human writings. But ritual traditions are either universal or particular. The former have a general foundation in Scripture ([[1 Corinthians 14:40 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:40]]), and so are called unwritten traditions only by catachresis — and these we necessarily and gladly receive. But the particular ones, as the name itself shows, could and should vary according to the variety of times, places, and persons, and therefore we judge that they do not oblige the universal Church of Christ.

title: Six reasons unwritten papal traditions cannot equal Scripture
english: The first reason is that they are deceitful and uncertain in many ways. First, as to origin. For many things can happen, as Peter de Soto himself teaches in his Defense of the Catholic Confession against Brenz, from which it may justly come into doubt whether some tradition is apostolic. And Andreas Fricius Modrevius: It is no light error of certain theologians of our time who, under the title of ecclesiastical tradition, do not indeed try to lead us away from the Scriptures, yet give first place to traditions and last to Scripture. As if any strength and firmness could be in that consensus and in those traditions that do not rest on the authority of the Word of God — which yet can be shown not even to have been born from the Apostles by this very thing, if they disagree with and are severed from the divine Scriptures, to which all things must be examined, and which must be ratified and firm in the Church of God.

Second, as to number. For in the Ratisbon Colloquy, when ordered to exhibit a certain number of traditions, the papists would not — indeed could not — because they are doubtful of it and do not agree among themselves about it, since some refer to traditions those heads of doctrine which others try to build from the Scriptures. Third, as to discrepancy: because some of the older fathers referred customs whose origin could not easily be shown to the Apostles, as if handed down by them — which yet Chemnitz proves from other writings of the ancients not to be apostolic.

The second reason is that they were proper to the Pharisees and to heretics, as is plain from [[Matthew 15:2 >> Bible:Matthew 15:2]]–7; [[Mark 7:3 >> Bible:Mark 7:3]]–8; Irenaeus Against Heresies 3; Chrysostom on Matthew; Josephus; and Peter de Soto the Dominican in his Defense of the Catholic Confession against Brenz's Prologomena.

The third: because even if it were most certain that some unwritten traditions of Christ or of the Apostles remain, equal authority with Scripture could not therefore be given them. For to things that are from the same author the same authority belongs only when the author put it in and willed it to be in them — who, as an agent acting freely, not of necessity but of free choice, puts more or less authority in his things, and hands some down forever and simply, some for a time and in a certain respect. But God uniquely authorized those things which He handed down to us in writing through the prophets and Apostles, because He handed down Scripture as the perpetual and perfect canon of this our life, in which alone is all that is necessary for the man of God to be perfect ([[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]).

The fourth: because those unwritten dogmas that today set Christians colliding mostly fight openly with Scripture, which all Christians with one mouth confess to be the Word of God — as has been variously and solidly shown by the Protestants, and they are condemned as figments of the human heart ([[Matthew 15:6 >> Bible:Matthew 15:6]]–9; [[Mark 7:7 >> Bible:Mark 7:7]]; [[Galatians 1:8 >> Bible:Galatians 1:8]]; [[Colossians 2:8 >> Bible:Colossians 2:8]]).

The fifth: because no sufficiently fit cause can be given why those things which men desirous of eternal salvation equally ought to know had to be partly written and partly unwritten, since God equally willed the help of Scripture for men's institution and memory in all things — unless perhaps we foolishly affirm that of those things which are equally necessary to salvation some are to be learned and committed to memory more lightly, others more accurately.
The sixth: because those very unwritten dogmas, without the support of some Scripture, neither were kept nor could have been kept, as the papists themselves confess.

title: Bellarmine's three heads of the tradition controversy; papists as twin rabbis
english: X. But Bellarmine sets this controversy in three heads (On the Word of God, book 4, chapters 3 and 4). The first is that the papists assert that all necessary doctrine, whether of faith or of morals, is not expressly contained in the Scriptures, and therefore besides the written Word of God an unwritten Word of God is required — that is, divine and apostolic traditions. So teaches John of Deventer in The Dart of Christian Truth, or Catapult of the Faith: The Church holds very many things not produced in dead letters, but written by the Holy Spirit in human hearts. To these as firm a faith is to be given as to evangelical Scripture, since it is agreed they were inspired by the same Spirit by which the Gospel was. It is therefore plain as a third truth that not all things to be believed and equally to be kept have been set out in the sacred letters. So Jodocus Clichtove in Anti-Luther book 1, chapter 4; John Fisher, bishop of Rochester; Peter de Soto; Alfonso de Castro of Zamora; Albert Pighius of Kampen; Martin Perez de Ayala, bishop of Guadix; Gregory of Valencia; and countless others. See the refutation in Whitaker and our Chanier, solidly and at length; briefly but with nerve in the Synopsis of purer theology, disp. 6, by the most celebrated D. Polyander, and, Bellarmine being unnerved, by D. Ames and others.

But here the papists are twin brothers of the rabbis, clinging to a double law from Moses — one written, the other by tradition — and branding as heretics those well versed in the Bibles, under the name of letter-men, textualists, biblical men, as Sadducees who, given only to the reading of the Bibles, clung to the written law alone, traditions rejected. But that the Apostles did not openly communicate to all their hearers all that God had revealed to them, but handed some things secretly and to a few as pertaining to the whole Church — Tertullian in the book On Prescription calls that madness.

XI. The second is that we think the Apostles did indeed institute certain things besides Scripture that pertain to the rites and order of the Church, which yet are not necessary for all Christians, nor commanded, but free; but the papists acknowledge apostolic traditions of every kind — that is, not only particular but universal, which are to be kept and handed down to the whole Church, as is to be seen in Bellarmine of the same book, chapter 3. See the refutation in the authors praised and in disp. 4 of our Anti-Bellarmine college, question 2.

XII. The third is that we teach that apostolic traditions, if they ever existed, do not now exist — that is, it cannot be certainly shown that any tradition is apostolic; but the papists assert that there is no lack of sure ways by which apostolic traditions are shown, in Bellarmine of the same book 4, chapter 9. But these are uncertain, obscure, and deceitful, as ours have clearly shown on this book of Bellarmine and elsewhere. Confer the praised disputation of the Anti-Bellarmine college, question 3.

title: Second contradiction: zealots who demand equal faith for private interpretations and consequences
english: XIII. Second, certain zealots contradict — not in the faith of charity, in which no zeal is too little, but in knowledge, that is, in those controversies in which even the pious can sometimes easily err — who demand that their interpretations and certain consequences, though notoriously not received in the Church in every age, be believed equally with the Word of God.

Such men, though they wish to appear to have made a secession from the Papacy, can scarcely, while this opinion of theirs stands safe, defend against the papists that the Scriptures alone are the clear and sufficient canon of the faith: namely if they will that whatever they themselves, by an interpretation and consequence not that catholic one granted by all, but a controversial one peculiar only to certain doctors, think can certainly be deduced from the Scriptures, must necessarily be believed. For in every consequence something of reason is assumed toward the testimony expressly in the Scriptures. And that natural assumption, unless it is common to all the pious, or even to all sound men, and so among them to the pious too, is not certainly and notoriously divine, equipollent and as it were understood under the Scriptures, but belongs to the στοιχεῖα καὶ κόσμου — the elements of the world ([[Colossians 2:8 >> Bible:Colossians 2:8]]). Those who use this therefore add to the Scriptures, and by that very thing open a gaping gate to all for inventing new heresies daily. For there will be no one who does not think some argumentation of his own to be necessary and evident.

title: Third contradiction: diverting the Church from the Bible to endless volumes; two modes of containing revelation; Cap. 5 close
english: XIV. Third, all contradict by the very deed who, not compelled by duty and the singular necessity of the Church, but stirred by the common itch of writing, already from the time of the Apostles onward, all first love — or the practice of the saints fully described in the sacred letters — set aside, miserably turn the Church of Christ by their πολυλογία from the richest and most wholesome storehouse of the Bibles to the poverty and leanness of their own volumes to this day.

For the sacred Bibles, which we still call so, are that one richest and most sufficient book and canon which, all the rest going into sponge or pyre, alone is more than enough for the worship of God and the salvation of men, even if not the least apex is set to it by a human finger — if only the true and apostolic practice of the saints, and the laborious charity of Christian faith and piety, painted in that book in full colors and graphically enough, is recalled by right of postliminium into use by the bishops and curators of the churches, by Christian magistrates, and by men of every order desirous of eternal salvation, in place of so many glosses, exegeses, interpretations, disputations, commentaries, reconciliations, elucidations, summas, commonplaces, catechisms, Articles, symbols, councils, confessions, postils, and like books, of which there is neither measure nor end, and under whose burden the Christian world groans. For if the pious consult the skill in church histories and controversies which they possess, they will without doubt discover that for no better cause than the omission of first love ([[Revelation 2:4 >> Bible:Revelation 2:4]]) the wrath of God, the candlestick moved, so heavily presses upon the church of the New Testament under the Smyrnaean, Pergamene, Thyatiran, and our Sardian condition, that scarcely greater likeness remains between these periods and the Ephesian, in which the Apostles themselves taught, than between lambs and pups — while in place of the true and practical knowledge of God with which the apostolic church was lit, bare heresies and their refutations, fights of words and quarrels of the schools have so prevailed, the efficacy of faith and the practice of piety more and more failing, that the light of the divine letters itself has been judged so dark, obscure, and insufficient, and the foremost of Christians, after the manner of the Israelites over the Baals, almost forgetting the Lord, have mostly begun to seek life from the dead and light from darkness — whether the Pope's or their own.

XV. For the rest, what is revealed in the sacred letters is contained in two ways: one expressly (αὐτολεξεί), according to the thing expressed to us by the signed words; the other virtually (δυνάμει), according to the thing though not expressed in signed words. The former mode, as it has sound words ([[1 Timothy 6:3 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:3]]), so those words must also be kept and the Apostle's rule held in them ([[2 Timothy 1:13 >> Bible:2 Timothy 1:13]]) — since, though Augustine witnesses (City of God 10.23) that philosophers speak with free words and do not fear offense to religious ears in things hardest to understand, yet it is right for us to speak by a fixed rule, lest license of words also beget an impious opinion about the things signified by them.

But the latter mode has words which, if newly employed by the Church so that by them a thing not so spoken may be expressed, must not be repudiated, provided the thing signified by them is brought into the letters. Of this kind is the Trinity, the Homoousion of the three persons of the Godhead — of which Augustine treats thus (tract. 97 on John): Against the impiety of the Arian heretics the fathers coined the new name Homoousion, but they did not signify a new thing by such a name. For this is called Homoousion which is: I and the Father are one — namely of one and the same substance. But whichever way God reveals some dogma, it makes no difference as to truth and infallibility, since it is agreed that both are truly had from the Holy Spirit. And lest anyone be troubled by the ambiguity of αὐτολεξεί, it is taken in two ways. First, rhetorically, and so it is the same as literally proper, when a certain word is taken properly and not modified and is opposed to tropically. Second, hermeneutically, and so it is the same as literally expressed, when the word by which a dogma or some thing is signed is had in the sacred writings, in whichever signification that is done — which is how we assert that many things must be believed that are not written in so many express words, provided the thing itself is in the Scriptures: to elicit which the fathers long ago judged that a true reasoning is needed.
